citeinfo.title: Geodetically improved images and mosaics of Titan via rigorous photogrammetric control of Cassini Imaging Science Subsystem data

descript.abstract: Saturn’s moon Titan is a focus of scientific investigation and future exploration by NASA’s Dragonfly mission. Its surface is covered by lakes of liquid ethane and methane, vast dune seas, and abundant organics sourced from photochemical reactions in its dense atmosphere. Over the course of its 13-year mission, NASA’s Cassini spacecraft’s Imaging Science Subsystem (ISS) acquired near-global imaging of Titan’s surface at a wavelength of 938 nm. At this wavelength, the methane that dominates Titan’s thick atmosphere is sufficiently transparent that, after extensive image processing, surface features can be discerned. From this data we generated a global photogrammetric control network consisting of 6,896 ISS images. The network included 92,831 tie points and more than 4.5 million image measures. The images are tied to Cassini Synthetic Aperture Radar data, which establish Titan’s geodetic reference frame. Least squares bundle adjustment was used to solve for tie point locations (latitude, longitude, and radius) and spacecraft (i.e., Cassini) position. Final control point uncertainties were < 600 m in latitude and longitude and < 800 m in radius. Due to the challenges resulting from generally low image signal-to-noise ratios and Titan’s diffuse surface features, hazy atmosphere and dense clouds, the network is effectively pixel-registered, rather than sub-pixel: two-sigma (95th percentile) tie point location residuals were ~1.1 pixels. Using a subset of these photogrammetrically controlled images, we generated a global mosaic. To further improve the uniformity of the mosaic and visibility of surface features, images were weighted by incidence angle and CCD position, and areas of low incidence and emission were trimmed. A 3131-pixel high pass filter was applied to the resulting mosaic to sharpen surface features. Here we provide this mosaic in both equirectangular and polar projections at 702 m/pixel. We also release updated camera extrinsics and spacecraft ephemeris data for every image in the network as a Navigation and Ancillary Information Facility (NAIF) Spacecraft, Planet, Instrument, C-Matrix, and Events (SPICE) kernel. The control network in ISIS format, image list, and bundle adjustment statistics are also included, and these provide a starting point for additional control network development or improvements.
descript.purpose:
Saturn’s moon Titan is uniquely Earth-like. Beneath its shroud of clouds, the moon’s surface includes numerous lakes, dendritic networks of stream-like features, and eroded topography that indicate an active hydrologic cycle, with liquid methane and ethane filling the role that water does on Earth. Vast seas of low-albedo, linear sand dunes, likely composed of organic material, cover the mid-latitudes. The surface and atmosphere are active, with occasional precipitation events, erosion, and active sand migration. In addition, Titan likely contains a liquid water ocean in its deep interior. The complex photochemistry occurring in its methane-dominated atmosphere, the abundance of solid organics on its surface, and the presence of liquid hydrocarbon lakes makes Titan a laboratory of low-temperature prebiotic chemistry, and therefore a target for NASA’s up-coming Dragonfly mission.
Because of its dense atmosphere, the surface of Titan was only relatively recently revealed by NASA’s Cassini-Huygens mission (2004 – 2017), which acquired both swaths of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) “images” of the surface from Cassini SAR, and traditional visible images through a methane window at 938 nm from the Imaging Science Subsystem (ISS). Over the course of its 13-year mission, Cassini acquired near global imaging of the surface, enabling us to produce the first photogrammetrically controlled imaging dataset. This controlled data provides a foundational data set for Titan. With the images properly located with known precision, scientists and mission planners can utilize the individual images or mosaics to investigate Titan’s surface processes, integrate additional datasets (e.g., Visible and Infrared Mapping Spectrometer data), derive new topographic information, and plan future missions (e.g., Dragonfly).

attracc.attraccr: To the best of our knowledge all attributes are accurate. No formal attribute accuracy tests were completed.

dataqual.logic: To the best of our knowledge, the data is logically consistent. No formal logical consistency or topology tests were conducted.
dataqual.complete: The data set includes updates camera pointing and spacecraft emphemeris information for 6,896 Cassini ISS images of Titan. This is a subset of all available images (~19,000) acquired of Titan in the CB3 and MT1 filters. The mosaics provide nearly global image coverage of Titan.

horizpa.horizpar: Tie points within the Cassini ISS Titan polar control network have a horizontal uncertainty of 583 m in latitude and 572 m in longitude (RMS), respectively. This corresponds to RMS residuals of 0.83 pixels, with two-sigma (5th and 95th percentile) residuals of -1.15 and 1.17 pixels, and maximum residuals of 6.25 pixels. We therefore contend that the data is pixel-registered, rather than subpixel-registered. The image network is tied to Cassini SAR data, which establishes the geodetic datum for Titan, via 72 manually selected ground points.

vertacc.vertaccr: Tie points within the Cassini ISS Titan global control network have a vertical root mean square uncertainty of 772 m, with maximum and minimum uncertainty of 103 m and 1,002 m, respectively.
